hero_examples.label: Pirate-treasure opening
hero_examples.title: The Drowned Map
hero_examples.text: The map was tattooed on the dead captain's back, and the ink only appeared when the tide came in. By sunrise, three crews knew the secret, and one of them had already cut the body loose.

hero_examples.label: Ruins three-act outline
hero_examples.title: The Moving Temple
hero_examples.text: Act one: a guide leads a rival expedition to a ruin that appears only at dusk. Act two: the temple shifts between valleys, and the crew discovers the map is a living thing. Act three: the guide must choose between the treasure and the village the temple is heading toward.

hero_examples.label: Branching scene
hero_examples.title: The Sea Gate
hero_examples.text:
Scene: The sea gate opens beneath the drowned city, and the current pulls the boat toward a corridor of black water.
Choices:
1. Sail inside and trust the current.
2. Dive below and look for the gate's mechanism.
3. Turn back before the tide closes the entrance.

ideas_and_plots.title: Adventure Story Ideas & Plots
ideas_and_plots.intro: An adventure needs a destination, a cost, and an opposing force. Start with a goal the protagonist cannot reach safely, then make every route more expensive.
ideas_and_plots.twist_title: Adventure story ideas with a twist
ideas_and_plots.twist_intro: These premises give the generator a turn that changes what the journey was really about.

items.title: The map that is alive
items.description: The treasure map changes every night, and the route it draws is heading toward the protagonist's home.

items.title: The guide who is the treasure
items.description: The expedition is hired to protect a guide who turns out to be the only thing the rivals actually want.

items.title: The rescue that is a trap
items.description: A missing crew sends a distress signal, but the rescue party arrives to find the message was recorded years ago.

items.title: The shortcut with a price
items.description: A supposedly safe passage saves a week but requires the party to leave something behind at every gate.

writing_prompts.intro: Pick a setting and give the party a concrete goal. Each prompt below includes a destination, a danger, and a reason to keep moving.

items.prompt: A pirate captain races a rival crew through a drowned city for a map to an island that appears once a year.

items.title: Lost world

items.title: Space
items.description: A frontier with a deadline.
items.prompt: A salvage crew has six hours to strip a derelict ship before its orbit decays into a inhabited moon.

items.title: Fantasy kingdom
items.description: A journey through hostile politics.
items.prompt: A courier must cross a kingdom where every bridge demands a riddle and the answers are state secrets.

items.title: Survival
items.description: The environment is the antagonist.

items.title: Mystery quest
items.description: The destination keeps changing.
items.prompt: A guide leads a rival expedition to a temple that moves between valleys, and the map is written in the guide's own hand.

choose_your_own.title: Choose Your Own Adventure
choose_your_own.intro: Choose the branching outline length when you want the shape of a choose-your-own-adventure story without building an interactive app. The generator returns one scene and two or three numbered choices, each with a distinct immediate consequence.
paragraphs: Use the outline as a planning document. You can expand one branch into a full story, use the choices as a tabletop encounter, or turn each option into a separate scene.
The output is static text, not a clickable game. It does not track state, combat, inventory, or multiple players.
choose_your_own.example:
Scene: The sea gate opens beneath the drowned city.
Choices:
1. Sail inside and trust the current.
2. Dive below and search for the gate's mechanism.
3. Turn back before the tide closes the entrance.

branching_outline.title: Branching Story Outline
branching_outline.intro: A branching outline is useful when you need options rather than a single path. It keeps the scene concrete and makes each choice change the next problem.

steps.title: Set the scene
steps.description: Show where the protagonist is, what they want, and what is immediately in the way.

steps.title: Offer two or three choices
steps.description: Each choice should lead to a different consequence, not a different wording of the same action.

steps.title: Pick a branch to expand
steps.description: Turn your favourite choice into the next scene, or continue the outline in AI Write.

how_to.title: How to Generate an Adventure Story in 4 Steps
how_to.intro: Adventure is a chain of escalating costs. The four steps keep the journey from becoming a list of places.

steps.title: Setting
steps.description: Choose the world and the rule that makes travel dangerous.

steps.title: Inciting incident
steps.description: Give the protagonist a concrete goal and a reason they cannot wait.

steps.title: Escalating obstacles
steps.description: Make each route cost more than the last. The opposing force should adapt.

steps.title: Payoff
steps.description: Let the destination matter. The final choice should reveal what the journey was really about.

what_works.title: What Makes an Adventure Story Work
what_works.intro: Adventure is not just movement. It is a series of choices that become more expensive.

items.title: Escalating conflict
items.description: Each obstacle should remove an option or raise the price of the next one.

items.title: Cost
items.description: The protagonist should lose time, safety, trust, or a piece of the plan at every stage.

items.title: Maps
items.description: A map is useful when it creates a decision, not when it merely describes the route.

items.title: Goals
items.description: The destination should be specific enough that the reader can tell whether the protagonist succeeded.

comparison.title: Adventure vs Fantasy: Which Generator Do You Need?
comparison.intro: Adventure and fantasy overlap, but they promise different stories. Choose adventure when the journey and its costs are the point.
comparison.adventure: Adventure focuses on a goal, a route, escalating obstacles, and a payoff. The world can be any genre.
comparison.fantasy: Fantasy focuses on a world with magic or mythic rules. The journey may be part of it, but the fantasy rule is the engine.

definition.title: What is an Adventure Story Generator?
definition.intro: An adventure story generator turns a setting and a premise into a plot, a short story, or a branching outline. It is a drafting tool for journeys, not a game engine.
paragraphs: The useful output is the chain of choices. A good adventure gives the protagonist a concrete goal, makes every route cost something, and ends with a payoff that changes what the journey meant.
Use the draft to test the structure. Check that the obstacles escalate, replace generic locations with your own details, and make sure the ending depends on a choice rather than a coincidence.

faq_section.name: faq
faq_section.label: FAQ
faq_section.title: Frequently Asked Questions
faq_section.description: Common questions about the adventure story generator, the branching outline, and how to use the output.

items.title: Is there a free adventure story generator?
items.description: Yes. This page is free to start, with no sign-up required for the first generation. You can generate a one-line hook, a short story, a full plot, or a static branching outline.

items.title: Can I use it online without installing anything?
items.description: Yes. The generator runs in the browser. You do not need to install an app or create an account to start your first generation.

items.title: Can I play the story as a game?
items.description: No. The branching outline is static text: one scene and two or three numbered choices. It is a planning document, not an interactive game with state, combat, or inventory.

items.title: Can I make a text-based adventure RPG?
items.description: You can generate scenes and choices that could become part of a text-based RPG, but this page is not a rules engine. It does not track stats, items, or player state.

items.title: Can I generate a DnD adventure or campaign?
items.description: You can use the output as a hook, a location, or an encounter for a tabletop session. It is not a full campaign generator, and it does not include stat blocks or rules.

items.title: Can teachers use it with students?
items.description: Yes. The four-step structure (setting, inciting incident, escalating obstacles, payoff) works as a classroom planning exercise. Review the generated content before sharing it with students.
